---
name: oss-issue-draft
description: Draft a concise evidence-backed open source issue in the user's voice and stop before publication.
---

Draft an open source issue from the supplied finding or the most recent verified investigation in the conversation. If neither provides a concrete target, ask for the repository and finding, then stop.

1. Read the repository instructions, contribution guide, issue templates, AI policy, approval gate, and relevant current source before drafting. Preserve unrelated worktree changes.
2. Search open and closed issues, pull requests, discussions, commits, and compare branches for duplicates, prior decisions, active ownership, and fixes already on the target branch. Do not publish a duplicate or obsolete report.
3. Resolve the intended GitHub identity before preparing any public action. For an upstream issue tied to a personal fork or compare branch, default to the fork owner unless the user explicitly chooses another account. Immediately before publication, verify the authenticated API identity (for example, `gh api user --jq .login`); repository selection, Git remotes, and SSH host aliases do not select the issue author. If identity is ambiguous or mismatched, stop and ask the user.
4. Reproduce or otherwise verify every material claim. Record the affected version, target revision, environment, shortest steps, expected result, actual result, and a useful negative control when applicable. Clearly label anything not manually verified.
5. Preserve the user's real discovery journey when it adds credibility: what they noticed during ordinary use, what initially seemed unclear, where they looked next, and how source inspection or manual testing changed the diagnosis. Keep this first-person narrative concise and do not invent experiences, confidence, or test results.
6. Refresh the upstream target branch with a read-only fetch immediately before collecting references. For claims about current behavior, use the latest fetched target-branch commit—normally `upstream/main`—for every GitHub source permalink, with the smallest relevant precise line range. Add `?plain=1` before the `#L…` fragment on GitHub links to Markdown files so they open the referenced source lines instead of the rendered preview. Use an older revision only when the issue explicitly concerns that revision, and label it as historical. Link inline to public source, documentation, tests, history, and prior reports instead of citing local paths or mutable branch pages. Recheck the remote target tip immediately before presenting the final draft; if it moved, regenerate and re-verify every URL and line range.
7. Include screenshots, short recordings, logs, or traces only when they materially prove user-visible behavior that text cannot establish as clearly. Describe what each artifact proves, crop or redact private content, and never fabricate or upload evidence without explicit authorization.
8. Use the repository's required issue template and keep the body within its stated length expectations. Lead with the concrete change or symptom, explain why it matters, and present only high-confidence related findings that form one coherent scope. Use calibrated severity; do not call minor inconsistencies critical.
9. If a personal-fork compare branch exists, introduce it exactly as **“Proposed diff in my fork”**, link its upstream compare view, state its scope and validation, and treat it as a reviewable proposal rather than an authorized pull request. Do not claim a branch exists or is current without verifying it. Creating or pushing the branch requires separate explicit authorization.
10. Mention that the user can implement the change after the repository's required approval when applicable. Preserve required attribution and add a concise AI-assistance disclosure when repository policy or actual drafting assistance requires it.
11. Highlight trust-bearing notes with plain bold prefixes: **“Manual verification:”**, **“Proposed diff in my fork:”**, and **“AI assistance:”**. Keep each note factual and specific. Prefer these labels over blockquotes, GitHub callouts, or emojis; blockquotes are for actual quotations, and decorative emojis can make a first-person report look templated. Follow a repository-mandated style when it conflicts.
12. Output a proposed title and the exact issue body, followed by unresolved placeholders or evidence still needed. Keep the prose natural, direct, and close to the user's tone rather than over-polishing it into generic generated language.

Do not create, edit, close, label, react to, or comment on an issue; push a branch; open a pull request; or perform any other public or remote write. Show the exact target and final draft, then stop for the user's explicit confirmation of the specific next action.
